In a world filled with constant stimulation, boredom has acquired a bad reputation. Whenever we have a spare moment, we reach for our phones, eager to fill every gap with something entertaining. Yet boredom may be more valuable than we realize.

When we are bored, our minds begin to wander. This state, often called the default mode of the brain, is associated with creativity, self-reflection, and problem solving. Many great ideas have emerged not during intense focus but in moments of quiet, such as during a walk or a long shower. Boredom gives the mind room to make unexpected connections.

Boredom can also motivate us. It signals that our current activity is no longer meaningful, nudging us to seek new challenges and pursue goals that matter to us. Children who are given time to be bored often invent elaborate games and discover new interests.

Of course, this does not mean we should seek out tedium for its own sake. But learning to tolerate idle moments, rather than escaping them immediately, can lead to a richer inner life. Perhaps the next time you feel bored, you might simply let it be.
